restatements.text: Amends the California Constitution to authorize a one-time tax on the personal wealth and property of billionaires, creating a specialized reserve fund for the revenue that is exempt from state constitutional spending limits.

Allocates 90 percent of the tax revenues to a health care account and 10 percent to an education and food assistance account, and provides an initial $50 million loan to the Franchise Tax Board for administration.
Imposes a 5 percent excise tax on the net worth of applicable residents whose net worth is $1 billion or more for the 2026 tax year.
Establishes valuation methods for various asset classes, specifically exempting directly-held real property and establishing reporting requirements for privately held businesses and trusts.
Allows taxpayers whose tax liability exceeds the value of their publicly traded assets to open an Optional Deferral Account, deferring the tax payment until the assets are withdrawn or distributed.
Exempts the Franchise Tax Board from the standard Administrative Procedure Act rulemaking process for this tax until 2028.
Imposes penalties of up to 40 percent for gross understatements of tax liability and grants the Franchise Tax Board the authority to disregard transactions that lack economic substance.

Mandates an expedited judicial validation process for the act, requiring any challenges to be filed within 60 days in Sacramento County Superior Court, with direct appeal to the California Supreme Court.

analysis.answer: Current law was not provided, but generally California does not impose a state wealth tax. This measure creates a one-time 5% excise tax on the net worth of residents exceeding $1 billion.

Billionaires and their trusts will incur significant compliance costs, such as obtaining certified appraisals for privately held businesses, intellectual property, and other non-liquid assets to comply with the new reporting standards.

The costs fall exclusively on roughly 200 California billionaires. The primary beneficiaries are lower-income individuals receiving Medi-Cal, safety net hospitals, public school districts, and food assistance programs.

Wealthy individuals may attempt to avoid the tax by changing their state of residence before January 1, 2026, reallocating their portfolios into exempt asset classes like directly-held real estate, or initiating litigation to challenge the constitutionality of the tax.

The text asserts that federal funding cuts threaten Medi-Cal, education, and food programs, while noting that billionaires pay a disproportionately low effective tax rate on their accumulating wealth. The mechanism addresses this by levying a one-time massive wealth tax dedicated strictly to backfilling those specific shortfalls.

The Franchise Tax Board gains significant discretionary and rulemaking power because it is temporarily exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act and is authorized to redefine tax consequences by disregarding transactions it determines lack "economic substance."

The effect of state-level wealth taxes on the residency of the ultra-wealthy is disputed. Some researchers find that highly concentrated taxes on the wealthy lead to significant out-migration and capital flight, ultimately eroding the tax base. Other researchers find that billionaires are highly tied to their primary residence state due to business, social, and cultural networks, making actual out-migration in response to tax hikes statistically marginal.

Administration will be costly due to the intensive auditing and appraisal checks required for private assets, evidenced by the authorization of up to $50 million as a start-up loan for the Franchise Tax Board to build out the enforcement apparatus.
The measure includes an amendment restriction requiring a two-thirds vote in the Legislature, and any amendment must be consistent with and further the purposes of the Act.

flags.quote: (2) For purposes of this subdivision, a transaction or series of transactions shall be treated as lacking economic substance if the person does not have a valid and substantial nontax business purpose for entering into the transaction or series of transactions
flags.note: The term 'valid and substantial nontax business purpose' provides broad discretion to the Franchise Tax Board to invalidate transactions.

flags.quote: (c) Notwithstanding any other provision of the Constitution, the Act provides for taxation on all forms of personal property and wealth
flags.note: Overrides existing state constitutional rules regarding property taxation.

flags.quote: (8) The Board shall adopt regulations regarding the taxability of receivables and similar assets under this Part.
flags.note: The actual taxability of certain financial assets is delegated to future agency regulations.

flags.quote: (a) The provisions of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, also referred to as “the Act,” are severable.

The Legislature may amend the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, by statute passed in each house of the Legislature by rollcall vote entered in the journal, two-thirds of the membership concurring, if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.
flags.note: Imposes a supermajority threshold and a 'furthers the purposes' restriction on future legislative amendments.
